primitives.name: Streak Selection Bias Correction
primitives.verbatim_quote: Miller and Sanjurjo [8] pointed out that the GVT study - and many others that followed a similar analytical approach - suffered from the streak selection bias that appears in small samples (similar to the ones used in these studies) and essentially goes to 0 for infinite sequences.
primitives.assumptions: Finite sample size with binary outcomes (make/miss), independent and identically distributed shots.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Small sample sizes where selection of streaks introduces systematic underestimation of conditional probabilities.

layer2.mapping: Permutation-based correction adjusts empirical conditional probabilities to align with theoretical expectations under IID assumptions.
layer2.telemetry: Deviation of observed Pr[M|M] from expected 0.5 in finite sequences.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight emerges from the bias introduced when selecting streaks in finite sequences. When analyzing a fixed-length sequence of shots, if one selects a make at random and computes the conditional probability of the next shot being a make, this yields a systematically lower value than 0.5 due to selection bias. This is because a make that is selected must have at least one preceding shot, and the probability of that preceding shot being a miss increases the likelihood of observing fewer subsequent makes. The correction involves permuting the sequence of makes and misses to generate an empirical distribution of conditional probabilities under the null hypothesis of independence. By comparing the actual observed conditional probability to this distribution, one can assess whether the observed streakiness is statistically significant. This method addresses the failure mode of traditional analyses that do not account for the selection bias inherent in how streaks are sampled. The mathematical structure reveals a duality between the empirical and theoretical conditional probabilities, where the former is corrected by the latter through permutation. The implications extend beyond basketball into any domain where sequential binary outcomes are analyzed for patterns of dependence.
